execute: echo: true eval: true freeze: true editor: visual --- # Caveat emptor ## Caveats I will be showing you what you can do, not what you should do \br . . . Approaches shown today may be out of date by next week/month/year \br . . . Creating LLM tooling for phenotyping is easy, creating LLM tooling that improves the quality of research and provides a good user experience is hard \br . . . Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, for which task. \br . . . System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results. \br . . . Closed-weight models often show performance drift, making validation even harder. ## More caveats Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Antrhropic, etc) \br . . . And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources) ## Even more caveats Low quality health research is prevalent \br . . . Reproducibility crisis in health research \br . . . Impact of increased LLM adoption? Double-checking and adding context vs unreproducible black box .... # Working with LLMs from R ## Unstructured chat ellmer R package supports various popular providers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) chat <- chat_anthropic() chat <- chat_deepseek() chat <- chat_google_gemini() chat <- chat_mistral() chat <- chat_openai() ``` ::: ## Unstructured chat Similarly we can work with local models ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat <- chat_ollama() ``` ::: ## Unstructured chat I'm going to be using local MedGemma 4B today. You can choose a model you have access to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ellmer) library(dplyr) library(PhenotypeR) prompt <- "You are a clinical phenotyper defining study cohorts in real-world data. Be terse, cautious, and evidence-based." # chat_qwen <- chat_ollama( # model = "qwen2.5:0.5b", # system_prompt = prompt) chat_medgemma <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = prompt ) # chat_gemini <- chat_google_gemini( # model = "gemini-4-argon", # system_prompt = prompt # ) ``` ::: ## Unstructured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_qwen$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Hypertension encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations. Key features include: * **Elevated Blood Pressure:** Defined by consistent systolic (≥140 mmHg) or diastolic (≥90 mmHg) readings on multiple occasions. * **Signs & Symptoms:** * **Asymptomatic:** Often discovered during routine blood pressure monitoring. * **Headaches, Dizziness, Blurred Vision:** Suggestive of elevated intracranial pressure. * **Chest Pain, Shortness of Breath, Palpitations:** May indicate cardiovascular complications. * **Nosebleeds, Hematuria:** Can be associated with underlying vascular disease. * **Annoyance, Irritability:** Non specific signs of poorly controlled BP. * **Risk Factors:** Family history, age, race, obesity, sodium intake, physical inactivity, excessive alcohol consumption, and certain medications (e.g., NSAIDs, corticosteroids) can contribute. * **Comorbidities:** Diabetes, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome often coexist. The clinical presentation varies widely, with some individuals presenting with overt symptoms while others remain asymptomatic. A comprehensive assessment, including blood pressure measurement, clinical examination, and consideration of risk factors, is crucial for accurate diagnosis and management. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_gemini$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension") ``` ::: ## Structured chat ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_qwen$chat_structured( # "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", # type = type_object( # average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer() # ) # ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", type = type_object( average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer() ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $average_age_at_diagnosis [1] 60 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_gemini$chat_structured( # "Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension", # type = type_object( # average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer() # ) # ) ``` ::: ## Structured chat Remember, even with the same model you can get different results! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} chat_medgemma_new <- chat_ollama( model = "MedGemma:4b", system_prompt = prompt ) expected_age <- NULL for (i in 1:10) { cloned_chat <- chat_medgemma_new$clone() res <- cloned_chat$chat_structured( "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension", type = type_object( clinical_summary = type_string( description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation." ), average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer( description = "Estimated average age at diagnosis in years (positive integer between 1 and 100)." ) ) ) expected_age[i] <- as.integer(res$average_age_at_diagnosis) cli::cli_inform( "Turn {i}: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = {expected_age[i]}" ) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Turn 1: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 2: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 35 Turn 3: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 57 Turn 4: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 5: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 6: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 40 Turn 7: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 8: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 9: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 55 Turn 10: Expected age at clinical presentation of hypertension = 48 ``` ::: ::: ## Integrating tools ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_gemini$chat("What tutorial are we currently in?") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # current_tutorial <- function() { # "OHDSI Global AI Phenotyping Tutorial " # } # get_current_tutorial <- tool( # current_tutorial, # name = "get_current_tutorial", # description = "Returns the current tutorial we are in." # ) # chat_gemini$register_tool(get_current_tutorial) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # chat_gemini$chat("What tutorial are we currently in?") ``` ::: ## Structured chats + tools Note, tool-calling not supported in structured chats. Workaround is two steps 1) use tool in unstructed chat 2) follow up with structured chat # Principles ## Phenotyping tasks > A problem well stated is a problem half solved. \br . . . > Nowadays, a problem well stated is a problem 95% solved. ## Phenotyping tasks Today we're going to use LLMs for lower-stakes, human-in-the-loop, phenotyping tasks: - Drafting clinical descriptions \br . . . - Reviewing concepts to include \br . . . - Contextualising PhenotypeR results \br . . . Higher-risk topics we won't cover (maybe for next year): - Searching for codes. - Creating cohort logic. - End-to-end, black box, phenotyping # Clinical descriptions ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clinicalDescriptionSpecification() |> listviewer::jsonedit() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Specification ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyClinicalDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, "hypertension", tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//Rtmp6Teazq/hypertension.json ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $hypertension $hypertension$introduction_synonyms [1] "Hypertension is a chronic medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure. Other terms used include High Blood Pressure (HBP) and Hypertenion. It is a significant public health concern worldwide." $hypertension$clinical_presentation_and_symptoms [1] "Hypertension is often asymptomatic, with many individuals unaware they have it until complications arise. When symptoms are present, they may include severe headaches, nosebleeds, shortness of breath, anxiety, confusion, and vision problems. These symptoms are often associated with severely elevated blood pressure." $hypertension$epidemiology [1] "Hypertension prevalence increases with age. It is more common in men than women, but the gap is narrowing. Risk factors include obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, excessive alcohol consumption, smoking, and family history. Non-modifiable risk factors include age, sex, and race. Comorbidities associated with hypertension include cardiovascular disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure. It is also a significant risk factor for heart disease and stroke." $hypertension$assessment_diagnosis [1] "Diagnosis is based on repeated blood pressure measurements at the healthcare provider's office or other healthcare setting, ideally at the upper end of normal range to ensure accurate assessment. The average of multiple readings is used for diagnosis. Other tests are not routinely required for diagnosis unless there are symptoms that cause concerns." $hypertension$therapeutic_plan_treatment [1] "The initial treatment plan for hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes (such as a low-sodium diet) and regular exercise. If lifestyle changes are insufficient, medication is often prescribed. Common medications include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), diuretics, beta-blockers, and calcium channel blockers. The choice of medication depends on the individual patient's characteristics, including age, race, other medical conditions, and potential side effects. The goal of treatment is to reduce blood pressure to a target level, usually below 140/90 mmHg." $hypertension$complications_prognosis [1] "Uncontrolled hypertension can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular disease (such as heart attack and heart failure), stroke, chronic kidney disease, and vision loss. The prognosis for patients with hypertension depends on the severity of the condition, the presence of complications, and adherence to treatment. Early diagnosis and aggressive management of hypertension can significantly reduce the risk of these complications." $hypertension$disqualifiers [1] "Conditions that might mimic the symptoms of hypertension, or cause a similar presentation in patient’s might be considered alongside the initial diagnosis, and might be treated as separate diseases. These include heart failure, pheochromocytoma, and renal artery stenosis. These conditions are considered alongside the initial diagnosis but are then differentiated by other tests." ``` ::: ::: ## Drafting clinical descriptions using an LLM ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd <- draftClinicalDescription(chat_medgemma, c("Primary hypertension", "Secondary hypertension", "Resistant hypertension"), tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting clinical description for Primary hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Primary hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//Rtmp6Teazq/Primary hypertension.json Getting clinical description for Secondary hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Secondary hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//Rtmp6Teazq/Secondary hypertension.json Getting clinical description for Resistant hypertension using MedGemma:4b Exporting clinical description for: 'Resistant hypertension' ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//Rtmp6Teazq/Resistant hypertension.json ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Primary hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Primary hypertension, essential hypertension, benign hypertension, idiopathic hypertension" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Secondary hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Secondary hypertension refers to high blood pressure that is caused by another medical condition. Common synonyms include secondary essential hypertension and hypertension due to an identifiable cause." ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_cd$`Resistant hypertension`$introduction_synonyms ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure that remains elevated despite the use of three antihypertensive medications, including a diuretic, at optimal doses. Other terms used to describe this condition include resistant to treatment, treatment-resistant hypertension, and chronic hypertension that is difficult to control. In some cases, the definition may be modified to require the use of four antihypertensive medications." ``` ::: ::: ## Extra context: data source descriptions Data partner descriptions can be used to provide extra context ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shinyDataSourceDescriptions(directory = tempdir()) ``` ::: # Reviewing codes ## Reviewing codes To do # Contextualising PhenotypeR results ## Contextualising PhenotypeR results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_exp <- getCohortExpectations(chat_medgemma, "hypertension", tempdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Getting expectations for hypertension Exporting CSV with expectations for hypertension ✔ Exported as /var/folders/sw/rd8zn92n2nz45cfcc5dcs_080000gr/T//Rtmp6Teazq/expectations.csv ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} hypertension_exp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # <script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
